body_markdown:
Mountains of parts exist within my medium-sized garage. Over the years, I have made a significant effort to pack 15 pounds into the 5-pound bag that is the garage. With the acquisition of a few new storage items, I now have the excuse to shuffle everything and look at many of the parts that are normally buried from sight and decide if they get to stay.


As a bonus, I get to create a system that provides easier access to everything, which means less stuff will disappear into storage for another five years untouched. All this made me think about what I was keeping and what methods I was using to let things go. Here are four takeaways.


## Only keep usable items


It’s a lot of shelf space, but there are certainly parts I don’t need to be holding onto in here.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Especially with old cars, we who work on them will sometimes buy a new part, get the car functioning, and then decide to hang onto the part we’ve replaced. Surely it has value and deserves to be kept.


Not so fast. If it was due for replacement, why keep the worn-out part? One might be able to make an argument for holding onto it temporarily to confirm the new part indeed fixes whatever problem was occurring, but after that it has served all of its utility. I am no stranger to finding an old used water pump in my parts stash, and every time it forces me to question my sanity. When would I ever bolt a used water pump up with confidence? I replaced it for a reason, then kept it… for no reason.


This is also true for scrap materials. Not all project cars require fabrication, but should you get involved in making your own solutions, beware of the scrap trap. The small offcuts of exhaust tubing or six inches of fuel line that surely will have a use in the future. I can’t recall the last time I needed just a few inches of hose. When I do, oftentimes finding that perfect offcut is harder to find or work with than just cutting a fresh piece from new stock.


## Store in ready-to-use condition


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Lots of the stuff on my shelves came from parts cars or motorcycles, meaning they were in rough condition when I got them. While it’s often easiest to store everything in assembled form, the parts machines I bring home often have only a[handful of good bits](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/the-best-break-from-a-big-project-is-another-project/) and a lot of items destined for the recycling bin.


It’s important to sort through what parts I bring home, and more importantly, ensure they are actually usable and will remain that way during storage. I don’t have enough space to store junk, and if I’m looking for a part in storage, the last thing I want to do is dig through a mountain of greasy stuff that looks and feels like junk. Cleaning and inspecting parts immediately ensures that my stored stock looks and feels like the valuable stuff that it is.


## Avoid the “but it’s worth something” trap


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


There are a lot of things gathering dust on my shelves that are worth a few bucks, but fascinatingly they are basically worthless to me. The tissue dispenser that was attached under the ashtray of my 1965 Corvair when I bought it has value to someone who likes neat options of the 1960s. I’m not that person, yet I hold onto this piece like it’s an investment. I won’t be using it, and am more likely to damage it in storage than anything. Really, this should be removed from my storage and placed into the hands of someone who actually wants it. And the stuff that isn’t worth anything—and won’t be worth anything, even as a reference piece—is likely best shuffled off for recycling. It’s hard to let stuff go, but remember that if we as humans built that piece once, we can certainly build it again.


## Set a clock to revisit/re-clean


This corner is typically full of spares and parts. Pulling everything out helps keep it from overflowing.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I know that last line was tough to read; I’m glad you didn’t skip straight to leaving a comment, because I’m here to offer a compromise. Go ahead and hold onto that thing that feels irreplaceable or like it will be salvageable in the future—but put a clock on when the future is. I try to go through and clear out some of the chaff from my parts stash[every two to three years](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/the-real-project-that-never-ends-your-garage/) simply because my interests tend to shift, and I find myself looking for space and am therefore more willing to part ways with certain parts or even tools. The joke is that I should just build more space, but unfortunately that’s not in the cards, so it’s down to self-control to keep the space functional and tidy. Periodic reviews and going-throughs help make a small space work harder.
